name: Einstein's Cluster
description: A static ball of particles on circular orbits in every direction, each held on its circle by the gravity of all the others, with no pressure along the radius. Einstein built it in 1939 to argue that no body can be squeezed inside its Schwarzschild radius, and it now serves as a model for halos of dark matter.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Picture a swarm of bees in the shape of a ball, each bee flying a circle about the middle, the circles tilted every which way so that the swarm as a whole turns in no direction. Albert Einstein built a star on that plan in the spring of 1939, with gravity doing the work of the hive: "a great number of small gravitating particles which move freely under the influence of the field produced by all of them together", each on a circular path about the centre, "a system resembling a spherical star cluster" [einstein1939]. He built it to answer a question: can real matter be packed so tightly that the sphere at its Schwarzschild radius lies bare outside it, the place where a clock at rest "would go at the rate zero" [einstein1939]? Karl Schwarzschild's ball of incompressible liquid gets there if it is made large enough, Einstein wrote, but he distrusted a liquid whose "elastic waves would have to travel with infinite velocity" [schwarzschild1916b, einstein1939]. A cluster needs no equation of state [einstein1939].¶Einstein sent the paper off from the Institute for Advanced Study, and it was received on 10 May 1939 [einstein1939]. A particle on a smaller circle must fly faster, and close to a compact mass the required speed reaches that of light [einstein1939]. In Einstein's isotropic coordinate that happens at $2 + \sqrt{3}$ times the radius of the Schwarzschild sphere, which is one and a half Schwarzschild radii in the areal radius [einstein1939, bonolis2017]. No circle fits inside, so a cluster stays larger than that however its mass is spread, and Einstein concluded that Schwarzschild singularities "do not exist in physical reality", since "matter cannot be concentrated arbitrarily" [einstein1939]. He worked one cluster through in numbers, with a density falling as $1/r^2$ and every particle at one speed [einstein1939]. Squeezed from infinite size it gives up at most about 5 percent of its mass, and squeezing it further takes energy [einstein1939].¶On 1 September of that year J. Robert Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder published the collapse of a ball of dust, which by its own clocks falls through its Schwarzschild radius in a finite time [oppenheimersnyder1939, bonolis2017]. Einstein's clusters are the ones that hold still, so the bound on their size says nothing of a body that has stopped holding still [bonolis2017]. The historian Jean Eisenstaedt called the argument circular: orbits assumed to be circles cannot lie inside one and a half Schwarzschild radii to begin with [bonolis2017]. Einstein thanked Howard Robertson, Valentine Bargmann, and Peter Bergmann for discussions of "the mathematical and physical significance of the Schwarzschild singularity" [einstein1939, bonolis2017]. Robertson showed, in work he did not publish, that a body in free fall crosses the Schwarzschild sphere in a finite time by its own clock [bonolis2017]. According to Bergmann, Einstein did not know of Oppenheimer's papers [bonolis2017].¶The cluster's next reader, C. Gilbert, took it in 1954 for what it resembles, a globular cluster of stars, and rewrote it in the areal radius [gilbert1954]. Asking which orbits are stable, he found a cap on the particles' speeds that in most cases leaves the cluster weighing less than the sum of its particles [gilbert1954]. Then came the quasars, whose redshifts Fred Hoyle and William Fowler proposed in 1967 to be gravitational: light climbing out of a deep well at the centre of a cluster of dense, burned out stars [hoylefowler1967, zapolsky1968]. Harold Zapolsky put the proposal to the test on Einstein's cluster a year later [zapolsky1968]. An orbit too deep inside a compact cluster is unstable: with $m(r)$ the mass inside the radius $r$, as a length, a circular orbit holds only where $r > 6m(r)$ [zapolsky1968]. A stable cluster with a redshift of 2 at its centre then has to be some 3600 times denser there than on average, which he found hard to square with the observations and with how star clusters evolve [zapolsky1968].¶What holds a cluster up? Nothing pushes outward along its radius: the sideways motion of the particles acts as a pressure across the radius, and that pressure alone balances gravity, as the stones of a dome hold one another up [cardoso2022]. The simplest example dates from 1974, when Petros Florides wrote down a ball of uniform density with no stress along its radius, joined smoothly to Schwarzschild's metric at its surface [florides1974]. Under certain conditions, he wrote, it "may be interpreted as the field inside an Einstein cluster" [florides1974]. Space inside it is a cap of a three sphere, as it is inside Schwarzschild's liquid star of the same density [schwarzschild1916b, bohmerlobo2008]. Christian Böhmer and Francisco Lobo followed the cap out to the equator of the sphere, where the stress and the curvature grow without limit and the particles move at the speed of light [bohmerlobo2008].¶Einstein's numerical example came back as a model of dark matter [einstein1939, bohmerharko2007]. A cluster whose particles share one speed has a mass that grows in step with the radius, which is what the flat rotation curves of galaxies ask of a halo [bohmerharko2007]. The proposal that halos are Einstein clusters of weakly interacting massive particles is Kayll Lake's, from 2006 [lake2006]. Such a cluster, he showed, reproduces the rotation curve of any galaxy once the angular momenta of its particles are chosen to suit, and the halo "is supported by the hoop stresses created by the orbiting WIMPs" [lake2006]. A year on, Christian Böhmer and Tiberiu Harko found these halos stable under small disturbances and a slightly weaker lens than the isothermal sphere usually assumed [bohmerharko2007]. A cluster of 2022 has a black hole at its centre: Vitor Cardoso, Kyriakos Destounis, Francisco Duque, Rodrigo Panosso Macedo, and Andrea Maselli built it in closed form, shaped like a galaxy, and found that to leading order the galaxy redshifts the gravitational waves from its core [cardoso2022].

related.text: The static sphere with both of its functions free. The cluster is the star whose pressure along the radius vanishes, which ties the redshift function to the mass, $\partial_r\Phi = m/(r(r - 2m))$ [lake2006, cardoso2022].

The vacuum outside the cluster. Einstein found that no circular orbit of a material particle fits inside one and a half Schwarzschild radii, so the cluster never uncovers $r = r_s$ [einstein1939, bonolis2017].

The other ball of uniform density. Space inside it is the same cap of a three sphere as inside Florides's cluster, held up by a pressure that is the same in every direction, and Florides called his own "a new interior Schwarzschild solution" [schwarzschild1916b, florides1974, bohmerlobo2008].

The answer from the same year that came out the other way. Oppenheimer and Snyder let a ball of dust fall, and it passes through its Schwarzschild radius in a finite time by its own clocks [oppenheimersnyder1939, bonolis2017].

Einstein's first static ball of matter, from 1917: a whole three sphere of uniform density, held still by the cosmological constant. Florides's cluster is a cap of such a sphere, held still by the motion of its particles [einstein1917, bohmerlobo2008].

A static star of the same year whose fluid presses equally in every direction, with a density that falls as the square of the radius. Richard Tolman's paper was received on 3 January 1939, four months before Einstein's [tolman1939, einstein1939].
Another star whose stress along the radius differs from its stress across it, made of a scalar field with no particles circling [ruffini1969].
Another static ball with no surface, whose stress along the radius differs from its stress across it. It is made of Yang-Mills field and is known only numerically [bartnik1988, volkov1999].
The same support within one plane: a static disc of dust on circular orbits, half the grains circling each way. Morgan and Morgan cite Einstein's paper [morgan1969].

A star of dust held up by its electric charge. Bonnor and Wickramasuriya set it beside Einstein's cluster as a body of well understood matter, and its surface can lie as near its horizon as one likes [bonnor1975].

A star of uniform density with pressure both along the radius and across it. In the limit $Q \to 0$ of Bowers and Liang's exponent the pressure along the radius vanishes, and the star is Florides's uniform cluster [bowers1974, florides1974].

coordinates.name: Areal Radius

parameters.description: Redshift function, dimensionless: a clock held at radius $r$ runs at $e^{\Phi}$ of the rate $t$ counts. Outside the cluster $e^{2\Phi} = 1 - 2GM/(c^2r)$, which fixes the constant it would otherwise carry

Mass function, a length: $m = GM(r)/c^2$ with $M(r)$ the mass inside the sphere of radius $r$, so $\partial_r m = 4\pi Gr^2\rho/c^2$ for the density $\rho$, and $m(0) = 0$. Any $m(r)$ with $3m < r$ is a cluster, whose particles circle at the fraction $V$ of the speed of light, $V^2 = m/(r - 2m)$, and whose redshift function follows from $\partial_r\Phi = m/(r(r - 2m))$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. The mass function $m(r)$ is a length and is left free, and the redshift function $\Phi(r)$ is dimensionless, with $\partial_r\Phi = m/(r(r - 2m))$ where no pressure acts along the radius. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Constant Speed

parameters.description: Speed of the particles as a fraction of $c$, the same at every radius, $0 < V < 1$
Areal radius of the cluster, where it joins Schwarzschild's metric with $r_s = 2V^2R/(1 + 2V^2)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius, inside a cluster of radius $R$ whose particles all circle at the fraction $V$ of the speed of light. Its mass function is $m = V^2r/(1 + 2V^2)$, and $t$ is the time of Schwarzschild's metric outside. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Isotropic (Einstein)

parameters.description: Einstein's constant $\sigma_0$, the mass inside a sphere over twice its isotropic radius, dimensionless, $0 < \sigma < 2 - \sqrt{3}$; the particles circle at the fraction $V$ of the speed of light, $V^2 = 2\sigma/(1 - \sigma)^2$
Isotropic radius of the cluster, Einstein's $r_0$, where it joins Schwarzschild's metric; its areal radius is $R = (1 + \sigma)^2\rho_0$
Einstein's $a$, the factor on the flat space of the isotropic chart, dimensionless
Einstein's $b$, the square of the rate of a clock at rest, dimensionless; at the surface it is Schwarzschild's $\left((1 - \sigma)/(1 + \sigma)\right)^2$

coordinates.convention: We use Einstein's coordinates $(t, \rho, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ the isotropic radius, a length, inside a cluster whose surface is $\rho = \rho_0$. The constant $\sigma$ and Einstein's $a$ and $b$ are dimensionless, and the areal radius is $r = (1 + \sigma)^2\rho\,(\rho/\rho_0)^{-2\sigma/(1 + \sigma)}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Uniform Density (Florides)

parameters.description: Areal radius of the cluster, $R > \frac{3}{2}r_s$; its density is $\rho = 3c^2r_s/(8\pi GR^3)$ and its mass function $m = r_sr^3/(2R^3)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius, inside a cluster of radius $R$ and uniform density. Its Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, and $t$ is the time of Schwarzschild's metric outside. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{r_s\,r\left(R - r_s\right)\sqrt{R - r_s}\sqrt{R^3 - r_s r^2}}{2R^3\left(R^3 - r_s\,r^2\right)}\dot{t}^2 + \dfrac{r_s\,r}{R^3 - r_s\,r^2}\dot{r}^2 + \dfrac{r\left(r_s\,r^2 - R^3\right)}{R^3}\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{r\left(r_s\,r^2 - R^3\right)\sin^2\theta}{R^3}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Hyperspherical

parameters.description: Radius of the three sphere that space inside the cluster is a cap of, $a = \sqrt{R^3/r_s}$ for a cluster of areal radius $R$ and Schwarzschild radius $r_s$
Polar angle of the surface of the cluster, $\sin\chi_0 = R/a$, with $\sin^2\chi_0 < \frac{2}{3}$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\chi$ the polar angle on a three sphere of radius $a$, so that the areal radius is $r = a\sin\chi$. The cluster of uniform density, of areal radius $R$ and Schwarzschild radius $r_s$, has $a = \sqrt{R^3/r_s}$ and its surface at $\chi = \chi_0$, and $t$ is the time of Schwarzschild's metric outside. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
